title: Quantum Cryptanalysis on Two Feistel-Type Constructions
authors: Yan-Ying Zhu, Bin-Bin Cai, Fei Gao, Song Lin
abstract: With the rapid advancement of quantum computing, the security of traditional cryptographic systems is facing significant challenges. As a fundamental component of symmetric cryptography, block ciphers have attracted increasing attention regarding their quantum security in recent years.   In this paper, we propose new quantum attacks on two Feistel-type constructions, i.e., New Structure IV and the lightweight block cipher LBlock, under the quantum chosen-plaintext attack (qCPA) model. First, we construct an 8-round quantum distinguisher for New Structure IV and perform an $r(r>12)$-round quantum key-recovery attack. Compared with Li et al.'s qCPA-based result presented at INSCRYPT 2024, our attack reduces the time complexity by a factor of $2^{n/2}$, where $n$ denotes the subkey length. Second, we design a 9-round quantum distinguisher for LBlock and extend it to an $r(r>15)$-round quantum key-recovery attack. The proposed quantum distinguisher covers one more round than Liu et al.'s automated-search distinguisher at ASIACRYPT 2025, which results in a $2^{16}$ reduction in the time complexity of our $r$-round quantum key-recovery attack on LBlock. Furthermore, by analyzing the structure of the round function and the key scheduling of LBlock, we reduce the subkey guess space for the 15-round attack from 76 bits to 52 bits, lowering the time complexity from \(O(2^{38})\) to \(O(2^{26})\) by a factor of \(2^{12}\).
summary: This paper analyzes the quantum resistance of two block ciphers, New Structure IV and LBlock, using the qCPA model. The authors propose quantum attacks that leverage quantum period finding and search algorithms. Crucially, they improve the attack complexity for LBlock by analyzing its key scheduling, significantly reducing the required subkey guessing space.
main_problem: The paper assesses the quantum security of two specific Feistel-type block ciphers, New Structure IV and LBlock, against quantum cryptanalysis.
main_result: The authors developed quantum key-recovery attacks for both ciphers, significantly reducing the time complexity compared to prior art by exploiting structural properties and key scheduling relations.
method: The attacks utilize quantum algorithms, specifically constructing quantum distinguishers based on periodicity (related to the Simon algorithm) and combining this with Grover search over the subkey space.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the theoretical security of classical symmetric cryptography (block ciphers) under the quantum chosen-plaintext attack (qCPA) model. The underlying mathematical tools involve quantum period finding and quantum search algorithms.
key_observables: Time complexity reduction factors (e.g., $2^{n/2}$), the number of rounds covered by the distinguisher ($r>12$ for New Structure IV, $r>15$ for LBlock), and the reduced subkey guess space (from 76 bits to 52 bits for LBlock).
important_parameters: The subkey length ($n$), the number of rounds ($r$), and the initial/final complexity bounds ($O(2^{38})$ to $O(2^{26})$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is conducted under the quantum chosen-plaintext attack (qCPA) model, and the success relies on proving the periodicity of the underlying functions derived from the cipher structures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum circuits for the Grover and Simon algorithms, and show the specific quantum distinguishers and key-recovery attack procedures for New Structure IV and LBlock.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the quantum threat to block ciphers. It then details the quantum attack on New Structure IV, leveraging periodicity. Subsequently, it focuses on LBlock, constructing a quantum distinguisher and refining the key-recovery attack by analyzing the key scheduling algorithm to reduce the search space.
why_interesting: While the topic is cryptography, the methodology heavily relies on quantum algorithms (Grover, Simon) and complexity analysis, making it relevant to the theoretical understanding of quantum computational limits.
